description: A multidisciplinary team combining AI, data science, and space science to turn microgravity combustion data into innovative insights for safer space exploration.
summary:
FireOrbit is a spacecraft fire-safety dashboard and AI assistant built on NASA’s Physical Science Informatics (PSI) combustion data. A preprocessing pipeline turns PSI investigation metadata, experiment records and PDF reports into a normalized knowledge base. A FastAPI backend and web dashboard let researchers rank investigations, explore and compare experiments, and find coverage gaps, such as Moon-cabin oxygen levels and reduced pressure. Its “Ask FireOrbit” assistant uses retrieval-augmented generation (RAG): hybrid keyword and semantic retrieval, with query routing for oxygen level, fuel and outcome, feeds Gemini. Answers come with cited sources, and a what-if tool estimates burn likelihood from the nearest observed experiments, not a made-up model.

Fire is one of the most dangerous risks on crewed missions, yet decades of microgravity combustion evidence sit scattered across reports and tables. FireOrbit makes that evidence searchable, comparable and traceable, so mission planners can see what is known, what is uncertain, and what still needs testing.
details:
FireOrbit: project details

What it does and how it works

FireOrbit turns NASA's Physical Science Informatics (PSI) combustion data into a decision tool for spacecraft fire safety. It has three layers.

1. Data pipeline. Scripts extract text and tables from PSI PDF reports, parse the ISA-Tab investigation files, and normalize the experiment CSVs. The output is a knowledge base of investigations plus normalized experiment records (fuel, O₂ %, pressure, flow, outcome). Each investigation is scored for relevance and for Moon-base applicability, grouped by safety pillar (Prevention, Detection, Suppression, Fundamental). Values the pipeline had to assume are flagged. The text is split into 4,518 chunks: 2,777 report pages, 1,589 experiment records and 152 investigation summaries.

2. Backend (FastAPI). It serves the dashboard data, ranking, comparison and coverage-gap analytics, and the AI endpoints.

  • Retrieval. Hybrid retrieval combines BM25 keyword search with dense vector search, merged by reciprocal-rank fusion. A rule-based query router turns phrases like "85% oxygen", "methanol", "self-extinguished" or "SAMER" into metadata filters. This lets the system answer counting questions ("how many tests…") from structured metadata instead of guessing.
  • Fallbacks. FireOrbit keeps working when parts of the stack are unavailable. If the vector index or embedding libraries can’t load (for example on a small free server), the backend switches from hybrid to keyword search over the same report and experiment chunks, and its /health endpoint reports which mode is active. If no Gemini key is configured, the API returns the retrieved passages without a generated answer. If the backend can’t be reached at all, the dashboard loads an offline data snapshot and the Ask tab searches it locally by keyword, with a status line showing which mode the user is in.
  • Answers. A Gemini model writes the answer only from the retrieved passages, with numbered citations. A no-answer gate means greetings and unsupported questions don't produce invented answers.
  • What-if engine. It estimates burn likelihood from the nearest observed experiments. It reports confidence and warns about extrapolation, missing pressure data and the lack of partial-gravity data.

3. Dashboard. A static web app has tabs for Overview, Rank, Explore data, Compare, Ask FireOrbit, and Gaps & Earth. It is deployed on Vercel and has a keyword-search fallback if the backend is unreachable.

Benefits

  • Evidence scattered across reports and tables becomes searchable and comparable in one place.
  • Every AI answer points back to its source document and page, so it can be checked.
  • The tool states its limits openly: assumed data, extrapolation, single-source results.
  • Gap analysis shows which conditions, such as Moon-cabin oxygen or reduced pressure, have little or no data.

Intended impact

The goal is to help mission planners, safety engineers and researchers see what combustion evidence exists for exploration environments, how reliable it is, and where new experiments are needed. It supports safer cabin-atmosphere decisions and better prioritization of future fire-safety testing. It is a research aid, not a certification tool, and the dashboard says so.

Tools and technologies

  • Languages: Python, JavaScript, HTML/CSS
  • Backend: FastAPI, Pydantic, Uvicorn
  • Data processing: pandas, PyMuPDF
  • Retrieval: rank-bm25, ChromaDB, sentence-transformers (BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 for local use), NumPy, and a lightweight retriever for serverless (BM25 plus precomputed Gemini embeddings)
  • LLM: Google Gemini via the google-genai SDK
  • Deployment and tooling: Vercel (static frontend plus Python serverless API), Git/GitHub, pytest
  • Hardware: no specialized hardware. It runs on a laptop, and the live site runs on Vercel's serverless platform.

What makes it creative

  • It combines semantic search, keyword search and structured metadata routing, so the system can reason over whole sets of experiments, not just a few text snippets.
  • The what-if tool uses nearest-neighbour evidence from real experiments instead of a black-box model, and it tells the user how far to trust the result.
  • The "Gaps" view reverses the usual question. It shows what the data cannot answer about the Moon, as well as what it can.
  • The retrieval stack was redesigned to fit serverless limits: large ML libraries stay local, while the deployed version uses small dependencies and precomputed vectors.

Factors considered

  • Trust and traceability: citations, an answer gate, and the model barred from using outside knowledge.
  • Data quality: flagged assumed and invalid values, and warnings when evidence is thin.
  • Domain relevance: Moon-base scoring and coverage of exploration-relevant oxygen and pressure ranges.
  • Evaluation: an evaluation question set (eval_set.json) with answerable and unanswerable questions, used to calibrate retrieval.
  • Deployment constraints: serverless size limits, optional API keys, and graceful fallback to keyword search.
